summary: Decode new words using taught sounds

education.outcome: Read an unfamiliar word made from taught sound–letter relationships, blending independently before using audio support.
outcomes: Recognise taught sound–letter relationships: connect a written letter or letter group with its corresponding sound.
Blend sounds to read words: move from identifying individual sounds to combining them into a spoken word.
Segment words for spelling: identify the sounds in a spoken word and select the corresponding taught letters.
Read connected text: apply decoding to short sentences, then reread with increasing accuracy and appropriate phrasing.
Monitor meaning: notice when a decoded word does not make sense, revisit it and explain the meaning of a short passage.
education.lesson: guided practice immediately after explicit phonics teaching, a short literacy rotation or targeted consolidation with a teacher.
education.evidence: accurate reading of new words, fewer prompts, successful blending and a brief explanation of the passage’s meaning. Game completion alone provides limited evidence.
education.transfer: Read different words on paper and spell a dictated word using the same correspondences.

name: Think in Parts
purpose: Students construct an explanation using drawing, voice, animation and interactive diagrams. Structured challenges require them to show a relationship, predict what happens when one part changes and revise after feedback. Teachers assess the accuracy and reasoning in the explanation.
guardrail: Show a student-authored explanation, not automatic AI answers. Include a clear assignment or explanation goal.

summary: Explain how parts affect a whole

education.outcome: Explain a causal relationship with a consistent diagram and narration, then justify a prediction when one component changes.
outcomes: Break a concept into meaningful components: identify the parts, stages or factors that matter.
Explain relationships: show how one part affects another, distinguishing a description from a causal explanation.
Choose an appropriate representation: use an arrow for movement, a sequence for change over time or a diagram for structure.
Coordinate representations: ensure narration, labels and animation communicate a consistent explanation.
Revise understanding: identify a missing link or contradiction and improve the explanation after feedback.
education.lesson: an initial diagnostic task, consolidation after an investigation or an assessed explanation near the end of a unit.
education.evidence: conceptual accuracy, connected reasoning and the ability to answer a follow-up question. Assess visual polish separately so sophisticated animation does not obscure weak understanding.
education.transfer: Explain a related example without replaying the finished presentation.

summary: Make and defend an informed civic decision

education.outcome: Recommend a feasible proposal using evidence from competing perspectives, accurate budget reasoning and an explicit trade-off.
outcomes: Identify the public issue: explain what needs deciding and which institution has responsibility.
Interpret stakeholder perspectives: distinguish a preference from the interests or circumstances behind it.
Evaluate proposals against criteria: consider cost, access, likely benefit, environmental effects and fairness.
Explain trade-offs: identify what becomes possible, what is forgone and who may be disadvantaged.
Participate in deliberation: question proposals, respond to objections and revise a position when evidence warrants it.
education.lesson: the application stage of a civics unit, after teaching the relevant decision-making body.
education.evidence: a recommendation supported by evidence, accurate budget reasoning and an individual explanation of the trade-off. Winning the vote is not evidence of stronger reasoning.
education.transfer: Write an individual recommendation for a different community issue and identify the responsible institution.

education.outcome: Make a comparison supported by systematically collected observations and state a limitation of the evidence.
outcomes: Ask an investigable question: turn broad curiosity into something observable or measurable.
Record consistently: use agreed categories, units, locations and sampling procedures.
Separate observation from inference: distinguish a count from an explanation for it.
Compare data: identify patterns between locations or across time.
Evaluate uncertainty: recognise incomplete identification, uneven sampling and the limits of a small dataset.
education.lesson: fieldwork preparation, outdoor data collection and subsequent discussion, or a repeated investigation across a term.

education.transfer: Repeat sampling at another location or time using the same method and reconsider the explanation.

name: TinkerTest
purpose: Students identify a testable question, choose an independent variable, hold relevant conditions constant and make a prediction. They run a virtual investigation, interpret results and revise a conclusion using numerical evidence. Teachers help students distinguish simulation results from claims requiring physical investigation.
guardrail: Clearly identify simulation and illustrative data. Isolate one independent variable and preserve controls. Do not present simulated outcomes as real measurements.

summary: Tell, listen and improve a clear story

education.outcome: Tell a connected oral story, identify a point a listener may not understand and improve that point in a second recording.
outcomes: Sequence events: establish a meaningful order and communicate it through language.
Connect ideas: use words such as “first”, “after”, “because” and “finally” appropriately.
Add useful detail: identify characters, settings and actions without relying on the listener seeing the pictures.
Adapt to an audience: include needed information and make references clear.
Listen and revise: identify confusion or missing information in a recording and improve it.
education.lesson: oral-language groups, preparation for writing, responses to shared texts or short formative assessments.
education.evidence: clearer order, precise references and a revision that helps the listener understand. Preserve early and later recordings for comparison against an explicit language focus.
education.transfer: Retell a new picture sequence to a partner and check what the listener understood.

name: Clue Canopy
purpose: Students investigate illustrated stories by selecting relevant textual clues and explaining what those clues suggest. They distinguish observation from inference, consider another plausible explanation and revise a prediction when new evidence appears. Speech, drawing and writing reveal reasoning without requiring a single predetermined interpretation.
guardrail: Evidence must come from visible story text. Do not reward guesses without reasons. Offer spoken, drawn and written explanations.

name: Instruction Impossible
purpose: Students write directions for a character that follows explicit steps. A test reveals missing information, ambiguous language or an incorrect sequence. Students use the visible result to revise their instructions, retest them and exchange challenges so a classmate can follow the final version.
guardrail: Focus on writing clear instructions, not coding syntax. Show recoverable funny consequences and a concrete revision.

outcomes: Sequence necessary actions: include steps in an order that makes the task possible.

summary: Revise writing with a clear purpose

education.outcome: Make a focused change that meets a stated writing goal, preserves intended meaning and can be explained in terms of its effect on the reader.
outcomes: Understand a revision goal: recognise clearer sequencing, stronger detail or better support.
Locate a weakness: identify a part of their own writing needing attention.
Choose an effective change: add, remove, reorder or replace material for a reason.
Compare versions: explain how the revision changes the reader’s understanding.
Transfer the strategy: apply it to another piece with less prompting.
education.lesson: the revision stage of a writing workshop, immediately after feedback or in a short teacher conference.
education.evidence: an improvement tied to the goal and a credible explanation of its effect. More words, longer sentences or more adjectives do not automatically indicate better writing.
education.transfer: Apply the same revision goal to a new piece of the student’s writing without sentence-level suggestions.
